meta.title: Leveraging parallel computing for a visual onboard attitude tracking algorithm on qualified space hardware

abstract: Earth Observation (EO) missions represent a vital component of the space industry and support a wide range of scientific, environmental, and commercial applications. These missions retrieve visual data from payload cameras to be then post-processed for on-ground analysis and relegate critical support functions to the spacecraft platform. However, the recent need for autonomy raises the possibility of exploiting that data as additional information for onboard perception using Earth-related cues. Nevertheless, algorithm design has to consider hardware constraints to ensure successful integration into qualified space systems. This article introduces a novel visual attitude tracking algorithm for EO missions that uses Earth images to retrieve a direct relative attitude measurement. The algorithm uses the SuperPoint keypoint extractor coupled with a brute force matcher to build frame-to-frame correspondences. Those are then exploited by a geometrical relative attitude estimation algorithm bulked with RANSAC for outlier rejection. Crucially, this algorithm is developed to run on the space-graded Class-1-qualified board GPU@SAT. Hence, the design considers the evident constraints brought about by space-qualified hardware but also accelerates computation by exploiting parallel computing through the provided soft-GPU environment. This article shows performance levels as estimation accuracy and computational runtime of this complex algorithm, enabled by GPU@SAT.

blocks.html: The use of accelerated computing in space is becoming essential to enable visual AI algorithms for onboard flight applications. However, commercial-graded acceleration platforms (e.g. GPUs) are generally not well suited for critical tasks in space missions due to their limited reliability in radiation environments and their significant impact on system mass, power, and cost budgets. In particular, Earth Observation (EO) missions represent an important asset for the space industry, and hence require maximum reliability. In this context, visual data retrieved by payload cameras may represent an additional source of information for perception. An image processing algorithm may use Earth images to extract informative features to be exploited in a tracking algorithm. The ultimate goal of the algorithm could be attitude tracking and it could represent a direct Earth-related source of information for the navigation subsystem that complements the measurements provided by the attitude and orbit determination subsystem (e.g., GNSS, star trackers). This could be needed for instance when higher reactivity and accuracy is required in pointing, where these direct Earth measurements may inform visual-servoing-based control. To enable this task, this algorithm shall target reliable space qualified hardware. In this scenario, this article presents a novel attitude tracking algorithm based on EO images, designed to run on the GPU@SAT board. GPU@SAT is a Class-1-grade space qualified board developed by IngeniArs, providing a soft-GPU OpenCL-based framework that enables parallel computing for space applications [1]. While space qualification introduces a series of constraints that limit performance, the design tries to exploit the full acceleration potential of the GPU@SAT soft-GPU board using parallel computing.
The algorithm is divided into three parts (see Figure 1):
1. Feature detection, description, and matching: processes two consecutive frames to establish a set of feature correspondences (labeled tracks)
2. Outlier rejection: exploits RANSAC to prune away outlier tracks

3. Attitude estimation: computes a final relative attitude via an iterative algorithm Feature detection and description are performed by SuperPoint [2]. The network processes incoming gray-scale frames and extracts salient keypoints from images sequentially. Then, the matching task is performed by using a brute-force matcher based on L2-distance between the SuperPoint descriptors. The choice of a brute-force matcher over a data-driven solution (e.g. SuperGlue [3] or Light- Glue [4]) is driven by deployability concerns. Indeed, a preliminary analysis outlined that the brute-force matcher requires a lower memory footprint and less computational effort than these two AI-based solutions, being a crucial consideration when targeting space qualified hardware.

The attitude estimation exploits tracks to estimate the final attitude. This process becomes robust to outliers via the RANSAC algorithm. To simplify the spacecraft-to-Earth attitude determination, available onboard information (i.e. GNSS and star tracker data) are used to inform the estimator about the spacecraft motion and the inertial attitude within the inference of relative attitude with respect to Earth. The algorithm used is a variation of the epipolar constraint, which is solved for rotation (this follows the work by Christian et al. [5], which instead aims at relative translation). The GPU@SAT implementation uses single-precision format in host and a Q8.8 quantization in the device. Singleprecision on host, run on Python at the current stage, is compliant with typical CPU hardware support (e.g. LEON [8]). The QM.N format [9] employed on device reserves M bits for the integer part and N bits for the fractional part in the storage integer, for a total of M+N used bits. Note that the Q8.8 number is stored in a 32-bit integer in our implementation, so it has more room for the integer part to prevent overflow in add and multiply operations. The number is obtained as:
where f is the single-precision number, q is the quantized number, << is the bit-shift (to the left) operator.

Common operations are implemented in the following way: add, subtract remain the same as integer operations; multiply appends a shift by N bits, i.e. a bit-shift (to the right): q1 ⊙q2 = (q1q2) >> N; divide features a dedicated soft implementation.

Our algorithm exploits feature-wise parallelization to fully utilize the multi-threaded environment at maximum capacity. To achieve this, it is developed for the GPU@SAT board within the OpenCL framework, leveraging a custom Python-based OpenCL Interface library [10] to accelerate runtime performance. Figure 2 shows how the various building blocks are divided in the implementation. Apart from the neural network, described in Section 1.2.3, the following blocks are implemented on the board:
• Brute-force matcher: 2D parallel threads along the two input descriptor arrays to compute all distances, best matches computed on host
• Sampson distance error: parallelization along the keypoints, takes the keypoints and the estimated [E] as inputs, and outputs the m-distances vector
• Epipolar condition function (and Jacobian): parallelization along the keypoints, compute the [Hk] matrix and the equation Jacobian, respectively.

The deployment of SuperPoint in the GPU@SAT framework follows the same process as in the single building blocks, constructing a chain of sequential blocks as a functionality of the OpenCL Interface library [10]. The process also contains a conversion from the ONNX format to the custom OpenCL format for implementation.

The conversion algorithm from ONNX to OpenCL first parses the ONNX model and checks for internal coherency. Then, for each node, it generates an initializer module containing metadata for the kernel build and input/output information. Those modules are stored in a sequential list in order of execution. Finally, it performs two optimizations: 1) it prunes away no-op nodes (e.g. reshape nodes) and leaf nodes not in the output list, and 2) it optimizes memory usage by minimizing number and size of buffers in the graph. The model is saved in a custom format that may then be loaded and built using an initializer that triggers the same routine as for the single kernel.

All ONNX nodes needed are implemented to be compatible with the GPU@SAT software. Some nodes cannot be computed as parallel kernels in the current version of the software because of race conditions or quantization issues. Therefore, they are implemented as delegates to be run on host. To speed up computations, the convolution node is optimized for particular configuration using the Winograd transform [11]. This increases speed by approximately 5 times but heavily increments memory usage (see Section 2). Finally, the memory optimization algorithm minimizes buffer allocations by using a lifetime-based algorithm that evaluates where each intermediate value is needed in the network and overwrites the buffer when its use ends downstream.

This section outlines the results obtained with the proposed algorithm. As it may be expected, there is an important trade-off between numerical and computational performance, respectively in terms of estimation accuracy and algorithm runtime. Here we highlight this trade-off by showing some relevant figures. We evaluate the performance of the algorithm with a Monte Carlo analysis. Samples consists of 20 different trajectories of 500 s duration each, to have reasonably long trajectories to test the algorithm and an acceptable variety of scenarios. Images are generated with the ABRAM software [12], a physical-based rendering engine able to generated radiometric-consistent images of the Earth over multiple bands. All trajectories are sampled to pass over land, as the algorithm does not work over sea patches at this stage with the currently employed Earth texture. Images over sea are discarded as they represent outliers for the algorithm application. In summary we process approximately 6500 image pairs.

Figure 3 shows a Monte Carlo test that demonstrates overall numerical equivalence between the GPU@SAT and Intel<sup>®</sup> Core<sup>™</sup>Ultra 7 155H, on a reduced set of 5 trajectories. For time reasons, all other numerical testing was performed locally, supported by this coherency result. Figure 4 summarizes relevant tests for the algorithm in different forms of escalating complexity in terms of quantization and implementation. As expected, the algorithm performs best when in full single-precision form, and when using LightGlue instead of brute force. Furthermore, reducing the maximum number of points that the brute force matcher can extract does decrement the overall accuracy of the algorithm. This introduces a trade-off with computational time, when looking at execution times on GPU@SAT in Table 2. Finally, concerning the neural network implementation, Table 1 shows some profiling comparisons on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060. The optimization pipeline manages to reduce memory footprint by approximately 50%. Also, Winograd convolutions reduce runtime by 5 times, though needing higher memory to store intermediate outputs.

blocks.html: This article presented a novel attitude tracking algorithm for EO missions that leverages parallel computing for acceleration. Also, we highlighted current limitations of space qualified hardware to embark AI models and heavy algorithms. Computational time and memory remain major drivers in algorithm selection and design for critical components, as space qualified hardware imposes strict constraints. Future activities of this project include: optimization and validation of the neural network implementation for GPU@SAT, inclusion of a registration step to initialize the tracker and refinement of the keypoint matcher for best performance and computational efficiency.
